title: Net operating income: the number every test is built on
summary: Net operating income is the rent a building actually collects minus the cost of running it, before loan payments and income tax. Lenders build every cash-flow test on it, so it must be built the lender's way.
body:
Net operating income, or NOI, is what a building earns after vacancy and running costs but before debt and income tax. Mr Shabazz, a lender will rebuild your NOI from scratch, and if their number is lower than yours, every other ratio in your package falls with it.

In plain English

Think of a building as a small business. Its sales are the rent tenants would pay if every unit were full. Some units will be empty some of the time, and some tenants will pay late or not at all. What is actually collected then has to pay for management, insurance, maintenance, property taxes, shared utilities and a reserve for big repairs. Whatever is left is net operating income. It is the money available to pay the loan.

NOI deliberately excludes two things: the loan payments themselves, and income tax. That makes it a property of the building, not of how the building is financed or who owns it. Two identical buildings have the same NOI whether one is mortgaged heavily and the other owned outright.

The professional framing: building NOI line by line

  1. Gross potential rent. Every unit leased at market rent for twelve months.
  2. Less vacancy and credit loss. An allowance for empty units and unpaid rent, based on the market's evidence, not on your hopes. Lenders often apply a minimum allowance even to a fully pre-leased building [unverified — lender-specific].
  3. Plus other income. Parking, storage, laundry, signage. Lenders discount income that is not contracted.
  4. Equals effective gross income.
  5. Less operating expenses. Management fee (usually a percentage of collected income), insurance, repairs and maintenance, property taxes, common-area utilities, security, cleaning, and a replacement reserve for roofs, lifts and systems.
  6. Equals net operating income.

The professional framing: underwritten NOI versus pro forma NOI

Your forecast is called the pro forma. The lender's version is the underwritten NOI, and it is almost always lower. The lender will typically use market rent rather than your target rent, a vacancy allowance at least as high as the market's, a management fee even if you plan to manage the building yourself, and a replacement reserve even in a new building. The gap between your pro forma and the lender's underwriting is usually where a loan is lost, so close it yourself before you submit.

The professional framing: stabilised NOI and timing

Lenders care about stabilised NOI, the income the building earns once it has reached its long-run occupancy, not the income in its first months when units are still being let. During lease-up, collected income is low and costs are already running, so a new building can lose money for a period even if its stabilised NOI is healthy. That shortfall has to be funded, usually from an interest and operating reserve built into the loan or from your equity. Lenders also look at the quality of the income: leases with long terms and creditworthy tenants are worth more than month-to-month rentals, and a building dependent on one tenant is riskier than one spread across many. Two buildings with the same NOI can therefore support different loans, because one income stream is more certain than the other.

A worked example

A hypothetical building has 10 units at US$1,000 a month each.

  1. Gross potential rent: 10 units times US$1,000 times 12 months is US$120,000 a year.
  2. Vacancy and credit loss at 7 percent: US$8,400. Collected rent: US$111,600.
  3. Other income, from parking: US$2,400. Effective gross income: US$114,000.
  4. Operating expenses: management at 5 percent of effective gross income, US$5,700; insurance US$6,000; repairs and maintenance US$8,000; property taxes US$5,000; common utilities US$4,000; replacement reserve US$5,300. Total: US$34,000.
  5. Net operating income: US$114,000 minus US$34,000, which is US$80,000 a year.

Now see how fragile it is. If the sponsor had left out management and the reserve, the forecast NOI would have read US$91,000, about 14 percent higher. A lender would put both back, and every loan test sized on the higher figure would shrink by the same proportion. Expenses are about 30 percent of effective gross income here, so a 10 percent fall in rent cuts NOI by more than 10 percent, because most costs do not fall with it.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is operating leverage: costs that stay fixed while income falls. Insurance, taxes and maintenance do not shrink when a unit is empty. In the example, a 10 percent drop in collected income, about US$11,400, reduces NOI from US$80,000 to roughly US$69,000 once the management fee adjusts, a fall of nearly 14 percent. That magnified fall is what a credit analyst's stress test is designed to reveal.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner computes coverage on gross rent, or on NOI without management and reserves. "I will manage it myself, so there is no management fee." The lender's view is that if you fall ill, sell, or default, someone must be paid to manage the building, and the bank must be able to afford that person. Include every cost a third-party owner would bear.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, build your NOI the way the lender will, before the lender does. Use market rent supported by comparables, a vacancy allowance from market evidence, a management fee and a replacement reserve, and get insurance and property-tax estimates in writing from a broker and the assessing authority. Show a one-page NOI build-up with the source of each line. Then show it again with rent 10 percent lower and costs 10 percent higher. If your conclusions survive both, your NOI will survive the lender's red pen. Professional sign-off required: a licensed appraiser or valuer for market rent and vacancy if a lender relies on them, and an insurance broker for the insurance cost.

A practical tip: label every line in your NOI build-up with its evidence, such as "three comparables, attached" or "broker quote, attached". A reviewer who can see the source of each number tends to accept it; one who cannot will substitute their own.
checklist: NOI equals effective gross income minus operating expenses, before debt and income tax.
Effective gross income is gross potential rent less vacancy and credit loss, plus other income.
Include management, insurance, maintenance, property taxes, common utilities and a replacement reserve.
Lenders underwrite NOI lower than your pro forma; close the gap yourself first.
Fixed costs magnify a fall in rent into a larger fall in NOI.
Label every line with its evidence.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A sponsor's forecast shows NOI of US$100,000 with no vacancy allowance, no management fee and no reserve. Gross rent is US$130,000 and listed expenses are US$30,000. A lender applies 6 percent vacancy, a 5 percent management fee on collected income and a US$5,000 reserve. What NOI will the lender use?
selftest.a: Collected rent: US$130,000 less 6 percent, which is US$122,200. Management at 5 percent: about US$6,110. Expenses: US$30,000 plus US$6,110 plus US$5,000, which is about US$41,110. Lender NOI: about US$81,090, roughly 19 percent below the sponsor's US$100,000, and every loan test shrinks accordingly.

apply: Build a one-page NOI for a hypothetical 12-unit building, labelling the source you would use for each line.
sources: Source: the parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Part 5. Loan-to-cost, loan-to-value, debt service coverage and debt yield are commercial lending tests, not law; the limits used here (65 percent, 1.20 times, 25 years) are hypothetical illustrations and actual lender limits vary [unverified — confirm with each lender]. Loan figures were computed with monthly payments on a standard amortising formula.

title: Loan-to-cost, loan-to-value and the appraisal
summary: Loan-to-cost caps the loan relative to what you spend; loan-to-value caps it relative to what the bank could sell the building for. Both depend on numbers the bank checks independently, especially the appraisal.
body:
Loan-to-cost compares the loan to what the project costs; loan-to-value compares it to what an independent appraiser says the finished building is worth. Mr Shabazz, a lender applies both, and the lower answer is the one you live with.

In plain English

A lender wants your money in the deal and a cushion of value under its loan. Loan-to-cost, written LTC, measures the first: what share of the total cost the bank is paying. Loan-to-value, written LTV, measures the second: how far the building's value could fall before the bank's loan is larger than what it could sell the building for.

The professional framing: loan-to-cost

LTC is the loan divided by total development cost. Total cost includes land, hard construction costs, soft costs such as design, permits, legal and financing fees, contingency and construction interest. An LTC limit of 65 percent means you must fund at least 35 percent of total cost with equity. Lenders argue about what counts as cost, especially land: some count land at what you paid, some at its appraised value, and some at the lower of the two [unverified — lender-specific]. Ask early, because the answer moves your equity requirement directly.

The professional framing: loan-to-value

LTV is the loan divided by the appraised value. For a construction loan the relevant value is usually the as-complete value, sometimes the as-stabilised value once leased. For a term loan it is the current appraised value. A 65 percent LTV limit means the building's value could fall by 35 percent before the loan exceeds it, which is the bank's protection if it has to sell.

The professional framing: the appraisal

The appraisal, called a valuation in many countries, is commissioned or approved by the lender, prepared by an independent licensed professional, and addressed to the lender so it can rely on it. A valuer typically uses three approaches: comparable sales of similar buildings, capitalising the building's income at a market yield, and the cost of replacing it less depreciation. For an income-producing building, the income approach usually dominates. In its simplest form, value equals NOI divided by a market capitalisation rate. An appraisal you commissioned yourself and addressed to yourself is usually not accepted by a lender, though it is useful for your own planning.

The professional framing: as-is, as-complete and as-stabilised

A development appraisal usually reports more than one value. The as-is value is what the site is worth today, with its approvals, before construction. The as-complete value is what the finished but not yet fully leased building would sell for. The as-stabilised value is what it would sell for once leased to its long-run occupancy. As-complete is normally lower than as-stabilised, because a buyer would discount for the lease-up still to come. Which value the lender applies its LTV limit to matters a great deal, and it should be stated in the term sheet. A lender applying 65 percent to as-complete value is more conservative than one applying it to as-stabilised value, even though the percentage looks the same.

A worked example

A hypothetical project has a total cost of US$1,000,000 and stabilised NOI of US$80,000 a year. Similar buildings sell at a capitalisation rate of 6.4 percent.

  1. As-complete value by the income approach: US$80,000 divided by 0.064 is US$1,250,000.
  2. The bank's limits are 65 percent LTC and 65 percent LTV.
  3. LTC cap: 65 percent of US$1,000,000 is US$650,000.
  4. LTV cap: 65 percent of US$1,250,000 is US$812,500.
  5. The lower figure binds: the maximum loan on these two tests is US$650,000, and equity must be at least US$350,000.

Now suppose the appraiser uses a 7.0 percent capitalisation rate instead. Value becomes US$80,000 divided by 0.07, which is about US$1,142,857, and the LTV cap falls to about US$742,857. LTC still binds at US$650,000. But at an 8.5 percent capitalisation rate, value is about US$941,176, the LTV cap is about US$611,765, and LTV now binds below LTC. A one-and-a-half-point change in the valuer's market yield has moved US$38,000 of the loan into your equity.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an appraisal that comes in below your cost. That means the market would pay less for the finished building than it costs you to build, so the project destroys value at completion. Lenders treat that as a serious warning, because it suggests either costs are too high, rents are too optimistic or the market is weaker than you think. Do not try to argue an appraiser up; find out which assumption differs from yours and test whether they are right.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner focuses on whichever ratio flatters the deal. "The loan is only 52 percent of value, so it is conservative." If the lender's binding test is LTC at 65 percent, the 52 percent LTV is irrelevant to the loan size. Always compute every test and find which one binds; that is the one to work on.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, build a total-cost schedule that includes land, hard costs, soft costs, contingency, financing fees and construction interest, and ask each lender how it treats land. Estimate value yourself three ways: comparables, income capitalised at a range of market yields, and replacement cost. Then compute both caps at each yield, and note the yield at which LTV starts to bind. That yield is your sensitivity to the appraisal. Professional sign-off required: a licensed appraiser or valuer acceptable to the lender; cost consultant for the cost schedule.

When the appraisal arrives, read the assumptions section first, not the headline figure. The rent, vacancy, expense ratio and capitalisation rate it used tell you exactly where it agrees or disagrees with your model, and where the conversation with the lender will go.
checklist: LTC equals loan divided by total development cost, including soft costs, contingency and interest.
LTV equals loan divided by the appraised as-complete or as-stabilised value.
Ask each lender how land is counted: at cost, at appraisal, or the lower of the two.
The appraisal must be independent, licensed and addressed to the lender.
Income value is NOI divided by a market capitalisation rate; small yield changes move value a lot.
Compute every test and work on the one that binds.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Total cost is US$2,000,000 and stabilised NOI is US$150,000. The lender's limits are 60 percent LTC and 65 percent LTV, and the appraiser uses an 8 percent capitalisation rate. What is the maximum loan, and which test binds?
selftest.a: Value is US$150,000 divided by 0.08, which is US$1,875,000. LTC cap: 60 percent of US$2,000,000, which is US$1,200,000. LTV cap: 65 percent of US$1,875,000, which is US$1,218,750. LTC binds at US$1,200,000, just below LTV; minimum equity is US$800,000. Note the appraisal is below cost, which a lender will question.

apply: For a hypothetical project, compute the LTC and LTV caps at capitalisation rates of 6, 7 and 8 percent, and find where LTV starts to bind.
sources: Source: the parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Part 5. Loan-to-cost, loan-to-value, debt service coverage and debt yield are commercial lending tests, not law; the limits used here (65 percent, 1.20 times, 25 years) are hypothetical illustrations and actual lender limits vary [unverified — confirm with each lender]. Loan figures were computed with monthly payments on a standard amortising formula.

title: Debt service coverage and debt yield
summary: The debt service coverage ratio divides net operating income by the full annual loan payment, principal and interest. Debt yield divides NOI by the loan amount and ignores the interest rate altogether.
body:
The debt service coverage ratio, DSCR, asks whether the building's income covers its loan payments with room to spare; debt yield asks how much income the building earns per dollar lent, whatever the rate. Mr Shabazz, DSCR is the test most likely to decide your loan when rates are high, and it must always be computed on full principal and interest.

In plain English

A lender wants the building's income to be comfortably larger than the payments on its loan. If the income is US$1.30 for every US$1.00 of loan payments, the coverage ratio is 1.30 times. The extra 30 cents is the cushion that absorbs a vacancy, a repair or a rent cut without missing a payment.

The professional framing: DSCR

DSCR is NOI divided by annual debt service, where debt service is the total of principal and interest paid in a year. Lenders set a minimum, commonly somewhere between about 1.20 and 1.35 times depending on asset type and market [unverified — commercial practice, confirm with each lender]. This course uses 1.20 times as its illustration.

Debt service depends on three things: the loan amount, the interest rate and the amortisation period, which is the number of years over which the principal is repaid. A longer amortisation means smaller annual payments, so a higher DSCR for the same loan. On a standard amortising loan, each payment covers that month's interest plus a slice of principal, and the slices grow over time as interest falls.

The professional framing: debt yield

Debt yield is NOI divided by the loan amount, expressed as a percentage. It contains no interest rate and no amortisation, so it cannot be flattered by a temporarily low rate or a long repayment period. Lenders like it for exactly that reason. It answers a blunt question: if the bank had to take this building, what return would its money earn from the income alone? Some lenders set a minimum debt yield alongside DSCR [unverified — lender-specific].

The professional framing: coverage over time

A construction loan is usually interest-only, but the lender sizes it on the coverage the building will achieve once stabilised and on full amortising payments, because that is the loan the building must eventually carry. A term loan's coverage covenant is then tested regularly, often each quarter or each year on trailing NOI. Falling below the covenant is a default event, even if every payment has been made on time.

The professional framing: why lenders want headroom

The minimum DSCR is not a target; it is the edge of a cliff. A building running at exactly the minimum has no capacity to absorb a rent cut, a vacancy, an insurance increase or a rate rise without breaching its covenant. Lenders therefore look for headroom above the minimum in the base case, and they test whether the ratio survives reasonable stresses. A useful self-check is to ask how far NOI could fall before coverage reaches 1.00 times, the point at which income only just covers payments. That distance, expressed as a percentage, is called the break-even margin. A building that breaks even after a 30 percent fall in NOI is far more resilient than one that breaks even after a 10 percent fall, even if both clear the same covenant today.

A worked example

A hypothetical loan of US$650,000 at 8 percent, amortised over 25 years with monthly payments. Stabilised NOI is US$80,000 a year.

  1. Annual debt service on a fully amortising basis: about US$60,202.
  2. DSCR: US$80,000 divided by US$60,202 is about 1.33 times. It clears a 1.20 times minimum.
  3. Stress: NOI falls 10 percent to US$72,000. DSCR becomes US$72,000 divided by US$60,202, about 1.20 times, exactly at the floor, with no headroom left.
  4. The misleading version: interest-only payments would be 8 percent of US$650,000, US$52,000 a year, giving a DSCR of about 1.54 times. That number looks safe and is not the test the bank will use.
  5. Debt yield: US$80,000 divided by US$650,000 is about 12.3 percent, whatever the interest rate.

So the same building and loan reads as 1.54 times, 1.33 times or 1.20 times depending on how honestly it is computed and stressed. The lender reads it as 1.33 times with a fragile stress case.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is floating interest rates on a tight coverage ratio. If the loan rate floats and rises from 8 to 10 percent, annual debt service on the same loan rises to roughly US$70,900 and DSCR falls to about 1.13 times, below the covenant, without the building performing any worse. Ask what rate the lender stresses at, and consider a fixed rate, a rate cap or a longer amortisation when coverage is thin.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner computes DSCR on interest-only payments, or on gross rent, and reports a comfortable ratio that the lender then cuts in half. Always use full principal and interest at the lender's amortisation and underwritten NOI after vacancy, management and reserves. If you present the honest number first, the lender stops looking for the trick.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, build a small table: NOI at base, minus 10 percent and minus 20 percent, against interest rates one and two points above the quoted rate, at the lender's amortisation. Mark every cell below the minimum. If the base case is close to the floor, you know before the bank does that DSCR will decide the loan, and next lesson shows the levers. Report debt yield beside DSCR; a healthy debt yield reassures a lender that your coverage is not simply a product of a cheap rate. Professional sign-off required: accountant or financial adviser to check the model's amortisation formula and assumptions before you submit it.
checklist: DSCR equals NOI divided by annual principal plus interest.
Common minimums sit around 1.20 to 1.35 times; confirm each lender's figure.
Longer amortisation lowers annual debt service and raises DSCR.
Debt yield equals NOI divided by loan; it ignores rate and amortisation.
Never compute DSCR on interest-only payments or gross rent.
Stress NOI and the interest rate together and mark every cell below the minimum.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: NOI is US$90,000 and annual debt service is US$70,000. What is the DSCR, does it pass 1.20 times, and what is the maximum annual debt service at a 1.25 times minimum?
selftest.a: DSCR is US$90,000 divided by US$70,000, about 1.29 times, which passes 1.20 times. At a 1.25 times minimum, maximum annual debt service is US$90,000 divided by 1.25, which is US$72,000.

apply: Build a three-by-three stress table for a hypothetical loan: NOI at base, minus 10 and minus 20 percent, against the quoted rate and one and two points above it.
sources: Source: the parent handbook, Banking and Project Finance, Part 5. Loan-to-cost, loan-to-value, debt service coverage and debt yield are commercial lending tests, not law; the limits used here (65 percent, 1.20 times, 25 years) are hypothetical illustrations and actual lender limits vary [unverified — confirm with each lender]. Loan figures were computed with monthly payments on a standard amortising formula.

title: Sizing a loan: find the test that binds
summary: A lender lends the smallest amount allowed by all its tests at once, and the test that produces the smallest number is the one that binds. Changing anything other than the binding test does not change the loan.
body:
A bank runs loan-to-cost, loan-to-value and coverage together and lends the lowest of the three answers. Mr Shabazz, find which test binds on your project, because effort spent improving any other test changes nothing.

In plain English

Imagine three gates, each set to a different width. The loan is as wide as the narrowest gate. Widening the other two does not let any more through. Each lending test is one gate: what you spend, what the building is worth, and what its income can repay. The narrowest one is the binding constraint.

The professional framing: sizing on coverage

Sizing on LTC and LTV is simple multiplication. Sizing on coverage works backwards. Divide NOI by the minimum DSCR to get the maximum annual debt service. Then ask how large a loan that payment can support at the lender's rate and amortisation. That loan is the DSCR-sized loan. Because the answer depends on the interest rate, coverage is the test that moves when rates move.

A worked example

Use the hypothetical project from this week: total cost US$1,000,000, as-complete value US$1,250,000, stabilised NOI US$80,000 a year. The lender's limits are 65 percent LTC, 65 percent LTV and 1.20 times DSCR, with 25-year amortisation and monthly payments.

  1. LTC cap: US$650,000. LTV cap: US$812,500.
  2. Maximum annual debt service: US$80,000 divided by 1.20 is about US$66,667.
  3. At 6.5 percent, that payment supports about US$822,793. LTC binds at US$650,000. DSCR on a US$650,000 loan is about 1.52 times, and 1.37 times with NOI 10 percent lower.
  4. At 8.0 percent, the payment supports about US$719,803. LTC still binds. DSCR on US$650,000 is about 1.33 times, and 1.20 times with NOI 10 percent lower.
  5. At 11.0 percent, the payment supports only about US$566,828. Now DSCR binds. DSCR on a US$650,000 loan would be about 1.05 times, and about 0.94 times under stress.
RateDSCR-sized loanBinding testDSCR at US$650,000
6.5 percentUS$822,793LTC1.52 times
8.0 percentUS$719,803LTC1.33 times
11.0 percentUS$566,828DSCR1.05 times

Read it slowly. At 6.5 and 8 percent, the loan is US$650,000 and equity is US$350,000. At 11 percent, the bank lends about US$567,000, and the sponsor must find about US$83,000 more equity. The same building is bankable on one set of terms and not on another, purely because of the rate.

Debt yield at a US$650,000 loan is about 12.3 percent at every rate, which is why lenders like it as a cross-check.

The professional framing: reading the table as a lender

Three things in that table matter to a credit analyst more than the headline loan. First, which test binds, because that tells the analyst which assumption to challenge hardest: costs and land value when LTC binds, the appraisal when LTV binds, NOI and the rate when DSCR binds. Second, how close the other tests are to binding, because a deal where all three are nearly equal has no slack anywhere. Third, the stress column, because a loan that is sized correctly today can become non-compliant the first time rents soften. An analyst who sees all three tests close together and a stress case at the floor will recommend a smaller loan even if the base case technically passes. Present the table yourself, with the binding test marked, and you control how that conversation starts.

The professional framing: the levers when coverage binds

  1. Lower the rate. A fixed rate, a rate cap, a different lender, or a subsidised or development-finance component.
  2. Lengthen amortisation. At 11 percent, moving from 25 to 30 years raises the DSCR-sized loan from about US$566,828 to about US$583,369, a gain of about US$16,500. Helpful, but smaller than people expect at high rates.
  3. Raise NOI. Higher rents supported by evidence, higher occupancy, lower operating costs, or additional income.
  4. Reduce the loan. More equity. Always available, always the most expensive lever for you.

When LTC binds, rate is worthless as a lever: a cheaper rate at 6.5 or 8 percent adds nothing to the loan, because the cost gate is already the narrowest. The lever there is cost itself, or how the lender counts land and soft costs.

One more caution on the levers. Raising NOI on paper is the cheapest lever to pull and the least convincing to a lender, unless the higher rent or lower cost is backed by evidence such as signed leases or a fixed management contract. A lender will simply underwrite the old figure if the new one is unsupported.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a deal that clears coverage only at full rent and the quoted rate. A credit analyst runs the stress column first. A building that drops to exactly 1.20 times with a 10 percent NOI fall, as at 8 percent above, is technically compliant and practically fragile; a committee will ask for more equity, a lower loan or more income evidence.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner negotiates the wrong lever. Spending weeks fighting for a quarter-point off the rate when LTC binds wins nothing. Spending weeks arguing about land value when DSCR binds also wins nothing. Identify the binding test first, then negotiate only the levers that move it.

How you will use it

Mr Shabazz, rebuild this table with your own project's figures and a lender's actual limits, at the quoted rate and at two higher rates. Circle the binding test in each row. Then write one sentence for each: "The binding test is X; the lever that fixes it is Y; it costs me Z." That sentence, said without the spreadsheet open, is the pass standard for this whole subject. Professional sign-off required: accountant or financial adviser to review the sizing model before it is relied on.
checklist: The loan is the lowest of the LTC, LTV and DSCR-sized answers.
DSCR sizing: NOI divided by the minimum DSCR gives maximum debt service, then solve for the loan.
When rates rise, DSCR is the test most likely to start binding.
Levers when DSCR binds: lower rate, longer amortisation, higher NOI, smaller loan.
When LTC binds, a cheaper rate adds nothing; work on cost or how cost is counted.
State the binding test, its lever and its cost in one sentence.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: Cost is US$2,000,000 and the LTC cap is 60 percent. NOI is US$150,000, minimum DSCR 1.25 times, and at the quoted rate and amortisation US$1 of annual debt service supports about US$10 of loan. Which test binds, and what is the loan?
selftest.a: LTC cap: US$1,200,000. Maximum annual debt service: US$150,000 divided by 1.25, which is US$120,000, supporting about US$1,200,000 of loan. The two tests bind together at about US$1,200,000, so the sponsor must improve both cost and coverage to raise the loan; minimum equity is US$800,000.

apply: Rebuild the three-rate sizing table for a hypothetical project and write the one-sentence statement of the binding test, its lever and its cost.

title: Week 3 review: the numbers that size a loan
summary: Six questions on NOI, LTC, LTV, the appraisal, DSCR, debt yield and the binding test. Work the calculations aloud before reading the answer.
body:
This week was the arithmetic of a lender's decision: build NOI honestly, apply every test, and find the one that binds. Mr Shabazz, work each calculation aloud, then check against the answer.

Question 1. What is net operating income, and name three costs a beginner most often leaves out.

Answer. NOI is effective gross income, meaning gross potential rent less vacancy and credit loss plus other income, minus operating expenses, before debt and income tax. The three most often omitted costs are a management fee, even when the owner plans to self-manage; a replacement reserve for large repairs, even in a new building; and a realistic vacancy allowance, even when the building is pre-leased. A lender will put all three back, so put them in first.

Question 2. Cost is US$2,000,000 and the lender's LTC cap is 60 percent. What is the maximum loan and the minimum equity?

Answer. Maximum loan: 60 percent of US$2,000,000, which is US$1,200,000. Minimum equity: US$800,000. Remember to ask how the lender counts land within total cost, because counting land at cost rather than appraisal, or the reverse, can move the equity requirement by a large amount.

Question 3. Why does a small change in the appraiser's capitalisation rate matter so much?

Answer. Because income value is NOI divided by the capitalisation rate, so value is very sensitive to it. On NOI of US$80,000, a 6.4 percent rate gives US$1,250,000 and an 8.5 percent rate gives about US$941,000. If LTV is close to binding, that change moves part of the loan into your equity. An appraisal below cost is also a warning that the project may destroy value at completion.

Question 4. NOI is US$90,000 and annual debt service is US$70,000. What is the DSCR, does it pass 1.20 times, and what is the maximum debt service at a 1.25 times minimum?

Answer. DSCR is about 1.29 times, which passes 1.20 times. At 1.25 times, maximum annual debt service is US$90,000 divided by 1.25, which is US$72,000. DSCR must be on full principal and interest at the lender's amortisation, never on interest-only payments or gross rent.

Question 5. Define debt yield and explain why a lender likes it.

Answer. Debt yield is NOI divided by the loan amount. It contains no interest rate and no amortisation, so it cannot be flattered by a cheap rate or a long repayment period. It tells the lender what its money would earn from the building's income alone if it had to take the building. On NOI of US$80,000 and a US$650,000 loan it is about 12.3 percent, whatever the rate.

Question 6. In this week's sizing table, NOI falls 10 percent at an 8 percent rate. What is the DSCR on a US$650,000 loan, and what would a credit analyst say?

Answer. About 1.20 times, exactly at the floor. The analyst would say the deal is compliant but fragile, with no headroom for anything else to go wrong, and would likely ask for more equity, a smaller loan, a fixed rate, or stronger income evidence such as signed pre-leases before recommending it.

A further point connects Questions 3 and 6. When the appraisal and the coverage test both sit close to their limits, the deal has two independent ways to fail, and a credit committee knows that a weak market usually pushes both at once: lower rents cut NOI, and the same weakness raises the capitalisation rate an appraiser applies. Correlated risks deserve more headroom, not less.

Recap

Everything starts with NOI, built the way a lender builds it: market rent, a market vacancy allowance, every operating cost including management and reserves. Fixed costs magnify a fall in rent into a larger fall in NOI, which is why lenders stress it. Loan-to-cost caps the loan against what you spend and loan-to-value caps it against what an independent appraiser says the finished building is worth; small changes in the valuer's capitalisation rate move value a long way.

Coverage divides NOI by full principal and interest, and it is the test most sensitive to interest rates. Debt yield is the rate-free cross-check. The lender lends the lowest of the answers, and the test that produces it is the one that binds. Only levers that move the binding test change the loan: rate, amortisation and NOI when coverage binds, cost when loan-to-cost binds, value when loan-to-value binds.

Notice too how the tests interact with the earlier weeks. A larger equity contribution, which Week 2 named as the factor carrying most weight, does two things here at once: it lowers loan-to-cost and it lowers debt service, so it improves both of the tests most likely to bind. That is why lenders value equity so highly. It is the one lever that moves every gate in the same direction.

Mr Shabazz, the pass standard for this week is a single sentence about your own deal, said aloud without the model open: the binding test is this, the lever that fixes it is that, and it costs me this much. Next week turns to where the bank sits in the capital stack, what counts as equity, the security package, guarantees and covenants.

One discipline from this week is worth keeping for every model you build: show your calculation, not only your answer. Write the formula beside every ratio, state the amortisation period and payment frequency, and keep the stress cases on the same page as the base case. A reviewer who can follow your arithmetic in a minute trusts the result; one who has to reverse-engineer it starts looking for mistakes, and usually finds the one you did not know was there.
checklist: NOI includes vacancy, management and reserves, before debt and income tax.
LTC is loan over total cost; ask how land is counted.
Income value is NOI over the capitalisation rate; small rate changes move value a lot.
DSCR is NOI over full annual principal and interest.
Debt yield is NOI over the loan and ignores rate.
The lowest test binds; only its levers change the loan.
head: Checklist

selftest.q: A lender offers you a quarter-point rate reduction or a 5 percent increase in the land value it credits. Your loan-to-cost test binds and coverage has comfortable headroom. Which do you take, and why?
selftest.a: Take the higher land credit. With LTC binding, a cheaper rate does not increase the loan at all, though it does lower your interest cost; a higher credited land value raises total counted cost or counted equity and directly raises the LTC-limited loan. Check the trade with your own figures, since the rate cut still saves interest over the life of the loan.

apply: Without notes, compute the LTC cap, LTV cap and DSCR-sized loan for a project you invent, and state which binds.
